extracted.intended_audience: NIH-funded and aspiring biomedical researchers, PIs, institutional research administrators, and policy-interested scientists
extracted.subtask_description: A commentary-style blog post and discussion thread about the NIH funding crisis, focusing on how grant review, institutional practices, trainee pipelines, and budgeting choices affect who gets funded and who stays in research. It collects practitioner opinions and informal standards about sustaining labs and writing/positioning grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a simple case for your idea
rubrics_metrics.description: "Translation: 'I don't know how to make a simple case for my idea.'" (Spiny Norman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals should present a clear, accessible argument. Specific Aims are malleable — the 'map' of the proposal need not exactly match the immediate operational territory; if the funded work leads to different but better outcomes, that can be used to write a new proposal or justify renewal. Avoid relying on the narrative "I'm too smart/edgy for NIH"; instead make the rationale plainly persuasive to reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riskiness versus conservatism in government funding
rubrics_metrics.description: "Too intellectual and risky for government funding" / the idea that government funding disfavors high-risk, highly intellectual projects (becca, commenters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that study sections and federal funders often prefer safer, incremental projects backed by preliminary data. If pursuing risky/novel work, provide strategies to reduce perceived risk (pilot data, staged aims, clear milestones) or accept that funding routes may be different (small exploratory awards, foundations, targeted RFAs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence in applying for funding
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only people who can survive in this environment are people who are absolutely passionate...and persistently apply for funding." (Waterland quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career survival often requires repeated submissions and resilience after rejection. Plan for multiple application cycles and build a portfolio of applications (renewals, new submissions, smaller awards) rather than relying on a single hit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary data and alignment with prior work
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals that are closely aligned with prior work and supported by preliminary data tend to score better than highly speculative ones (commenters' N=1 examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use solid preliminary results to demonstrate feasibility. If you propose a major shift, provide bridging data or explain how early milestones will de-risk the project. Incremental follow-up proposals often score better than very creative but unsupported leaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional environment/support ('environment' score)
rubrics_metrics.description: The institution's commitment and resources matter to reviewers — there is an 'environment' score that affects fundability (mytchondria: 'that pesky "environment" score').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the application documents institutional commitment (space, core facilities, cost-sharing, mentoring). Institutions that overreach (no real support) will be disadvantaged; reviewers consider whether the organization can actually support the proposed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: University fiscal responsibility and overbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities overbuilt lab space and infrastructure during budget doublings ('shopping mall' analogy by Paula Stephan); this can create unsustainable fixed costs when budgets stagnate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutional long-term sustainability before assuming continued external funding. When assessing an institution, consider debt service, maintenance costs, and whether recent construction was funded responsibly rather than as speculative expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft-money vs hard-money salary expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations that faculty cover large fractions of their salary from grants (examples: 70–100% expectations mentioned) create instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating job offers or institutional policies, determine the fraction of PI salary expected from grants and whether the institution provides bridge/hard-money support. Proposals and career plans should factor in the local salary model's risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and rules on PI salary and indirects
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations to cap PI salary contribution from NIH (e.g., 'PI salary needs to be limited to 50% max across all NIH grants') and concerns about high indirect rates ('institutes then sucks up the indirects (around 71%)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy proposals include capping NIH-paid PI salary and removing indirect costs on PI salary to change incentives. When budgeting and evaluating grants, be explicit about salary and indirect distributions and consider institutional effects of these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for bridge funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of bridge funding is repeatedly cited as a cause of lab and PI loss ('there's no money for bridge funding').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions and funders should plan for transitional support to prevent abrupt lab closures. Evaluate institutional policies on bridge funding and incorporate contingency planning into career strategies and grant-dependent budgeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size of trainee pipeline and 'replacement value'
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern that too many graduate students/postdocs are being trained relative to available faculty jobs ('trained 7 grad students... should one train more than replacement value?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing lab staffing/training plans or institutional graduate admissions, account for downstream employment opportunities. Funders and PIs should consider trainee career outcomes and balance training capacity with realistic career placements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund people, not just projects (alternative funding models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to fund investigators on multi-year portfolios/presets levels rather than piecemeal project grants (Robert, Grumble: 'individuals were funded directly... once every five years a scientist would submit a portfolio').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the potential of longer-term investigator-centric funding to reduce administrative load and support exploratory research. Consider mechanisms (review cycles, preset funding tiers, new investigator pathways) to avoid locking out early-stage researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study section familiarity, networking and field-switch penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Switching fields or lacking a network can disadvantage applicants because 'reviewers are not familiar with you or your work' and you lack invitations/visibility (Brain, commentators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If changing fields, plan to build credibility (collaborations, invited talks, preliminary data) and educate reviewers. For review-related strategy, cultivate networks and seek appropriate study sections where your work will be understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public messaging about science (media narratives matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media focus on breakthrough narratives and 'too smart and edgy' frames can misrepresent how science progresses and affect public & Congressional support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists and institutions should communicate the value of incremental, unglamorous research and training investments to the public and policymakers. Craft messages that translate long-term returns rather than only headline breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return on federal training investment and brain drain
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal investment in training can be lost if trainees 'leak out' and cannot continue to contribute to science — 'a pretty sizable lost investment' (Lady Scientist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating funding policy, include opportunity costs and consider metrics that track how many trainees remain in research and how societal returns compare to the investment. Institutions should monitor and plan for retention and alternative career supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFAs and their impact on the NIH portfolio
rubrics_metrics.description: "RFAs do not narrow the NIH portfolio, quite the opposite." (comment/linked note).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that targeted funding announcements (RFAs) change portfolio composition but may broaden activity in particular areas. Evaluate RFA effects on diversity of funded science and on existing investigator pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative productivity metrics for national systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions to compare Canada vs US on productivity per dollar, retraction rates, citation counts, and journal targets to evaluate system differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing national funding models or institutional strategies, use multiple metrics (productivity per funding dollar, quality indicators, career outcomes) rather than single crude measures. Comparative analyses can illuminate how salary/funding models affect research outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trainees-as-labor recognition and exploitation risks
rubrics_metrics.description: "Trainees are in fact the labor force... Tricking them into seeing themselves as 'trainees' is what underpins the exploitation of them as a class." (drugmonkey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing training programs and budgeting, explicitly acknowledge the labor role of trainees and provide fair compensation, career development, and realistic transparency about likely career paths to avoid exploitative structures.
